stories.topic: How Spotify Led Amit to Shoegaze and Back to an Old Love
stories.summary: While Amit was listening to a lot of Yo La Tengo, Spotify suggested a 'shoegaze' playlist, a word he had never heard. He let it play, and a band called Galaxie 500 grabbed him. That set off a flashback. In the early-to-mid 90s, one of his favourite alternative-rock bands was Luna, fronted by Dean Wareham, and he had a vague sense that Wareham had an earlier band. In an India where the shops sold Deep Purple and Michael Jackson, he had no way of finding it. That earlier band was Galaxie 500. Amit then explains the genre: guitar-heavy, feedback-drenched bands with indistinct vocals, whose guitarists stood still on stage staring at their effects pedals.
stories.insight: If you let an algorithm's random playlist run and follow whatever strikes you, it can pull you out of a musical comfort zone. It can also close loops that scarcity once left open, and the old music you couldn't get can return as a new passion.
stories.quote: They just stand there and the guitarist would be looking at his pedals near his feet all the time to produce his effects and therefore shoegaze.

stories.topic: What Are the Two Most Recent Songs You Know?
stories.summary: Ajay and a friend put a question to themselves: what are the two most recent songs you know? His instinctive answer was 'November Rain' from 1992. After thinking carefully, he found one song he knows and loves from 2017, Harry Styles' 'Sign of the Times', and one from 2018, which he couldn't name until Amit supplied it: 'Shallow' by Lady Gaga and Bradley Cooper. He credits YouTube Music for bringing him new music.
stories.insight: It is a quick, funny self-audit of how musical taste freezes at a certain age, and a reminder that newer artists can be very good if you give them a chance.
stories.quote: I actually thought carefully about it and I discovered I know one song, I know and love one song from 2017 and one song from 2018.

stories.summary: Amit retells a parable from Steven Pinker's Enlightenment Now. Two Russian farmers: Boris has a goat and Igor doesn't. Igor complains to the authority that this isn't fair. Asked what he wants done, he says: kill Boris's goat. Inequality is solved, and now neither of them has a goat.
stories.insight: Equality can be reached by making everyone poorer. This is why Amit insists that poverty, not inequality, is the problem worth solving. Redistribution feels virtuous, but it can leave everyone worse off.
stories.quote: And what do you have if you kill Boris's goat? That's the end of inequality. Right, and neither of them has a goat.

stories.summary: Amit supported the CAA protests, and he was heartened to see young people across India on the streets holding up the Preamble of the Constitution. What filled him with despair was that they held up Indira's version, which contains the word 'socialist'. When the words 'secular' and 'socialist' were debated in Ambedkar's time, he said no to both. On 'secular', his view was that if the value runs through every article, stating it is mere signalling. On 'socialist', his view was that the choice of economic system is for politics to decide, not the Constitution. Ambedkar himself then favoured a socialistic organisation, but he changed his mind by the 1950s. Amit notes that Chandra Bhan Prasad's two heroes are Ambedkar and Adam Smith.
stories.insight: Great thinkers contain multitudes and change their minds, so judge them by their full body of work. The fashionable reading of the Constitution quietly carries a word that, Amit argues, kept India poor.
stories.quote: What filled me with despair was that that was Indira's preamble, not Ambedkar's preamble. And Indira's preamble has the word socialism in it.

stories.topic: Sex Workers Push Back on a TV Panel
stories.summary: Amit recalls a talk show hosted by Barkha Dutt where Kiran Bedi took a moralistic line on prostitution. Actual sex workers on the show pushed back. They said they had entered the work willingly, that it was the best option open to them, and they asked who she was to patronise them.
stories.insight: Elite moralising about other people's choices removes their agency. Criminalisation pushes the trade into the underworld, where trafficking and coercion flourish and victims cannot turn to the police.
stories.quote: You know, we chose it as a best option open to us, and you let us make our decisions.

stories.summary: While Section 377 still effectively criminalised homosexuality, cops placed ads on online bulletin boards asking gay men to meet them. When the men turned up at a railway station, often Matunga, plainclothes cops met them and extorted them, threatening to tell their wives or fathers. They then walked the victims to an ATM and emptied their accounts. Amit wrote a column about this racket years ago.
stories.insight: Laws against victimless crimes don't just fail. They hand the state's own enforcers a tool for extortion against harmless people.
stories.quote: And they'd go with him to the ATM, they'd use his card, they'd empty it out.

stories.topic: When Banning Child Labour Pushed Children Into Worse Lives
stories.summary: Amit cites two follow-up studies. In Bangladesh, Oxfam found that 30,000 children were laid off from alleged sweatshops after Western activists complained, and many girls went into prostitution while many boys turned to crime. In Nepal, after a scandal over children making carpets, UNICEF found that 5,000 to 7,000 children were laid off and the girls almost uniformly went into prostitution. Amit notes that the journalists behind such stories never follow up. Only these studies did.
stories.insight: No parent wants their child in a factory. They send children to work because every other option is worse. A ban that feels virtuous can destroy the lives it claims to save, and the real cure is growth that lifts family incomes.
stories.quote: The girls practically uniformly went into prostitution. Their lives became worse.

stories.topic: The Degrowth Advocate With a Single Malt
stories.summary: At a recent party, a very successful professional from Hyderabad, sipping a single malt, told Amit he found the word 'degrowth' very attractive and that India had had enough growth. Amit told him that free speech is fine, but what he was saying was deeply immoral, because degrowth hurts the poor. He adds that every one percent rise in GDP gets about two million Indians out of poverty.
stories.insight: Degrowth is a textbook luxury belief: fashionable for those who have already escaped poverty, devastating for those who haven't. Two million people are real human beings, not a statistic.
stories.quote: I said you know, free speech is fine and please say whatever you want, but everything you're saying is deeply immoral because degrowth hurts the poor.

stories.topic: The Strongman Eventually Turns on His Rich Backers
stories.summary: Ajay argues that business elites who have skimped on understanding society often back the strongman, expecting favours. He gives examples. In Saudi Arabia, MBS led a shakedown of hundreds of rich people and seized their wealth. In China, Xi Jinping attacked the rich, partly destroying and partly expropriating them. In Russia, Putin went after the rich. Each billionaire believed he was the insider who would get special treatment, and for a while it seemed to work.
stories.insight: Populist leaders have often been bad for growth and for the very businesspeople who backed them. The only sustainable path for building firms is rule of law and liberal democracy.
stories.quote: And each individual billionaire at some point thought that no, no, no, I'm the insider I will get special favors by the government and for some time it seems to work. But in steady state it didn't.

recommendations.item: Nowhere Near
recommendations.creator: Yo La Tengo
recommendations.context: Amit has been listening to a lot of Yo La Tengo lately, and their songs seeded his shoegaze discovery.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a beautiful song and one of the great love songs.

recommendations.item: On Fire
recommendations.creator: Galaxie 500
recommendations.context: His formal first recommendation of the episode. He discovered it via a Spotify shoegaze playlist. It is Dean Wareham's band before Luna.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a brilliant album you've got to listen to, an old love finally found.

recommendations.item: Lunapark
recommendations.creator: Luna
recommendations.context: Luna was one of Amit's favourite alternative-rock bands of the early-to-mid 90s.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a great album from a band he loved.

recommendations.item: November Rain
recommendations.creator: Guns N' Roses
recommendations.context: Ajay's instinctive answer when asked for the most recent song he knows.
recommendations.reason: A 1992 song that marks where his musical sense of 'recent' had stopped.

recommendations.item: Sign of the Times
recommendations.creator: Harry Styles
recommendations.context: One of the two most recent songs Ajay knows and loves, from 2017.
recommendations.reason: A song he genuinely loves, and Harry Styles is called 'bloody good'. A reason not to look down on new music.

recommendations.item: Shallow
recommendations.creator: Lady Gaga and Bradley Cooper
recommendations.context: Ajay's 2018 pick. Amit supplied the title, mentioned some awesome covers of it, and joked that they should perform it together.
recommendations.reason: One of the only recent songs Ajay knows and loves.

recommendations.item: Troubled: A Memoir of Foster Care, Family, and Social Class
recommendations.creator: Rob Henderson
recommendations.context: Henderson's new book about growing up in foster homes, which Tyler Cowen also discussed on Marginal Revolution.
recommendations.reason: Highly recommended. Henderson, whom Amit calls a very fine thinker worth following, coined 'luxury beliefs', the idea behind this episode.

recommendations.item: Luxury Beliefs are Status Symbols
recommendations.creator: Rob Henderson
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes as the source of the term Amit defines at the start of the episode.
recommendations.reason: Gives the original framing: beliefs that confer status on the upper class while inflicting costs on the lower classes.

recommendations.item: Enlightenment Now
recommendations.creator: Steven Pinker
recommendations.context: Source of the Boris-and-Igor goat parable Amit uses to open the inequality section.
recommendations.reason: Shows vividly why chasing equality can mean making everyone poorer.

recommendations.item: On Inequality
recommendations.creator: Harry Frankfurt
recommendations.context: Cited while arguing that poverty, not inequality, is the problem.
recommendations.reason: A slim, great book that sets out the 'doctrine of sufficiency': define what is enough to live on and get everyone there. A philosopher's case for why that matters more than equality.

recommendations.item: The Communist Manifesto
recommendations.creator: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels
recommendations.context: Ajay suggests it as an exercise during the discussion of socialism.
recommendations.reason: The book ends with a checklist program for action, and you'll be astonished how much of it exists in modern India, which in many ways is the communist paradise Marx and Engels wanted.

recommendations.item: The Vision of the Anointed: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy
recommendations.creator: Thomas Sowell
recommendations.context: Amit reads a long passage from it while explaining why people hold luxury beliefs.
recommendations.reason: A great book whose subtitle sums up the episode. It shows that elites treating disagreement as sin rather than error is at least 200 years old.

recommendations.item: Defending the Undefendable
recommendations.creator: Walter Block
recommendations.context: Amit's closing reading recommendation. He says he might one day borrow the title for an episode.
recommendations.reason: Block, an Austrian economist, defends ideas considered beyond the pale, much as Amit has just defended sweatshops and legal prostitution. You don't have to agree, but it makes you think in different ways instead of swallowing a tribe's dogma.

recommendations.item: Bootleggers and Baptists: The Education of a Regulatory Economist
recommendations.creator: Bruce Yandle
recommendations.context: Cited in the discussion of alcohol prohibition.
recommendations.reason: A great essay showing that people who call for bans and the bootleggers who profit from them have aligned interests.

recommendations.item: The Economics of Child Labor
recommendations.creator: Kaushik Basu and Pham Hoang Van
recommendations.context: One of the studies Amit cites while arguing against blunt child-labour bans.
recommendations.reason: Calls it a great study. It helps work out the family income level at which children stop being sent to work, showing that growth is the long-term solution.

recommendations.item: Observations on International Labor Standards and Trade
recommendations.creator: Alan B Krueger
recommendations.context: Cited alongside Basu in the child-labour discussion.
recommendations.reason: Calls it another great study on the economics of child labour.

recommendations.item: Child Labor in the Global Economy
recommendations.creator: Eric V Edmonds and Nina Pavcnik
recommendations.context: Cited alongside Basu and Krueger in the child-labour discussion.
recommendations.reason: Calls it another great study supporting the case that prosperity, not bans, ends child labour.

recommendations.item: Why Children Labour
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column on child labour, which links the various studies he mentions.
recommendations.reason: Gives the full argument and evidence, including the Oxfam Bangladesh and UNICEF Nepal follow-ups.

recommendations.item: Laws Against Victimless Crimes Should Be Scrapped
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit says he has written pieces on victimless crimes and links this 2008 column.
recommendations.reason: The longer case that banning prostitution, betting and alcohol hands these activities to the underworld.

recommendations.item: The Matunga Racket
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: His old column on cops extorting gay men while Section 377 was in force.
recommendations.reason: Shows concretely how criminalising consenting adults breeds extortion.

recommendations.item: Raees: An Empty Shell of a Gangster Film
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: His review of Shah Rukh Khan's film, raised in the bootleggers-and-Baptists discussion.
recommendations.reason: Explains why the film gets it backwards. A real bootlegger would fund the prohibitionist politician, not fight him.

recommendations.item: Price Controls Lead to Shortages and Harm the Poor
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked for the price-controls section, which covers stents and Uber surge pricing.
recommendations.reason: The fuller argument that removing the price signal creates scarcity that hurts the poor most.

recommendations.item: India's Problem is Poverty, Not Inequality
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked for the inequality section.
recommendations.reason: Develops his argument that India's moral imperative is ending poverty through growth, even if inequality rises.

recommendations.item: Beware of These Five Fallacies! (Episode 45 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Referred to as 'our last episode' for the zero-sum fallacy and the 'double thank you' moment.
recommendations.reason: Background for why a positive-sum world separates poverty from inequality, and why free markets reward serving others.

recommendations.item: The Populist Playbook (Episode 42 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited for how words like 'populism' and 'nationalism' get misunderstood, and later for tribalism and the Republican Party's direction.
recommendations.reason: Groundwork for the point that 'socialism' is another misunderstood, toxic word.

recommendations.item: Poker and Life (Episode 38 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned while arguing that betting should be legal.
recommendations.reason: Where they discussed that all of life is a gamble and there is nothing immoral in gambling.

recommendations.item: The Citizenship Battles (Episode 152 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Srinath Raghavan
recommendations.context: Mentioned while discussing the CAA protests.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a great episode on the CAA.

recommendations.item: Caste, Capitalism and Chandra Bhan Prasad (Episode 296 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Chandra Bhan Prasad
recommendations.context: Mentioned while discussing Ambedkar's changing views.
recommendations.reason: A great episode with the Dalit thinker whose heroes are Ambedkar and Adam Smith.

core_ideas.explanation: Rob Henderson's term for fashionable opinions that give elites status while their costs fall on the poor. Amit pictures elites in air-conditioned rooms typing on MacBooks, choosing a fourth pair of luxury headphones, and proposing policies that hurt the poor. His antidote is Gandhi's test: before any policy, ask what it does to the poor. In a poor country like India, that is a moral question.
core_ideas.quote: Luxury beliefs are ideas and opinions that confer status on the upper class while often inflicting costs on the lower classes.

core_ideas.concept: Socialism Means Coercion, Not 'Good for Society'
core_ideas.explanation: Many people hear 'socialism' as 'caring for society', just as populism is confused with 'popular'. Amit's definition: the state owns much of the property and regulates the rest, so you are a subject rather than a citizen, and freedom is something the state grants. His lens is consent versus coercion. The 20th century was the history of socialism's failure, and in India socialism kept hundreds of millions poor for decades longer than necessary.
core_ideas.quote: I care deeply about consent. It has an absolute value. And socialism is equal to coercion.

core_ideas.concept: Poverty, Not Inequality, Is the Problem
core_ideas.explanation: In a zero-sum world, poverty and inequality would move together. In a positive-sum world, growth makes the poor richer and the rich richer still, so inequality can rise as poverty falls, as it did after 1991. The thought experiment: would you rather be poor in the USA, which is more unequal, or in Bangladesh, which is poorer? Tackling inequality calls for redistribution, which is easy to sell and makes you feel virtuous. Tackling poverty calls for growth, which in a poor country will inevitably raise inequality, and that is fine.
core_ideas.quote: In which of these two countries would you rather be poor, the USA or Bangladesh? And the answer everybody will say I would rather be poor in the USA.

core_ideas.explanation: Harry Frankfurt argues that what matters morally is not equality but whether everyone has enough. Define the level a person needs to live on and get everyone there. This works as a proxy for ending poverty, a goal Amit says every Indian government has failed to reach.
core_ideas.quote: The doctrine of sufficiency is that you define what is enough for a man to live on. Right, you define that. And then you try to get everyone to that level. That is what matters.

core_ideas.concept: 200 Basis Points and the Power of Compounding
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's response to people who say a little inequality-chasing won't hurt growth much. He uses illustrative numbers: a growth-hostile Indian policy setup yields about 2% per capita growth, and a pro-growth one about 4%. By the rule of 70, 2% means 35 years to double and 70 to quadruple. 4% means about 16 years to double and 32 to quadruple. Thirty-two years is within a young person's planning horizon, such as the show's editor Nomsita's. Seventy years is beyond imagining.
core_ideas.quote: You think only 200 basis points, but there's a power of compounding.

core_ideas.concept: Banning Victimless Crimes Feeds the Underworld
core_ideas.explanation: This luxury belief comes from the right: ban prostitution, betting, alcohol and, formerly, homosexuality. Bans don't end these activities. They push them to the underworld, where the cops are paid off, the rule of law doesn't reach, and trafficking, match-fixing and spurious liquor thrive. In the Netherlands, legal and regulated brothels mean sex workers have rights, pay taxes and face little crime. England legalises betting and taxes the houses, not the gamblers' winnings. Amit wants banks to offer betting the way they offer demat accounts. His line is that the left should accept freedom in the marketplace and the right freedom in the bedroom.
core_ideas.quote: Consenting adults should be free to do whatever they want with each other, as long as they're not harming anyone else.

core_ideas.explanation: Bruce Yandle's insight is that the moralist calling for a ban and the bootlegger profiting from it want the same thing: the activity stays illegal. So in the real world, the bootlegger funds the prohibitionist politician rather than fighting him.
core_ideas.quote: The person who calls for the ban will be working towards the same purpose as a bootlegger, the underworld guy who comes in and takes over.

core_ideas.explanation: Capitalism turns ugly when allied with state power. That is cronyism, where businesses use the state to keep competitors out. True free markets need the rule of law and little else, so the only way to get rich is to serve people, which makes every trade a 'double thank you' moment. Anti-capitalist elites attack the system while tweeting on capitalist platforms and ordering next-day delivery from Amazon.
core_ideas.quote: Pro-business and pro-market can mean opposite things.

core_ideas.concept: Respect the Agency of the Poor (Sweatshops and Child Labour)
core_ideas.explanation: People work in sweatshops because it is the best option open to them. Banning it removes that option and leaves worse ones. Child labour is horrible, but blunt bans pushed by Western activists have sent laid-off children into prostitution and crime. Studies estimate the family income above which children stop being sent to work. The long-term solution is growth.
core_ideas.quote: Those people chose to work in a sweatshop because it was the best option open to them. Respect their agency, respect their decision.

core_ideas.explanation: Prices signal scarcities and constraints and encourage people to produce more. In Amit's thought experiment, capping cars at Rs 10,000 would kill the industry and push the few remaining cars onto the black market. In real life, he tweeted that the price control on stents would cause scarcity, and it did, and people died. Banning Uber surge pricing means no car when you urgently need one to get to a hospital or catch a flight. These controls are the Yes Minister instinct at work: we must do something, this is something, let's do it.
core_ideas.quote: If you take that information away, you are always going to have scarcities.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay, a card-carrying economist, asks what the elites are optimising for. His hypotheses: it costs nothing once you are already rich. Pious views are old-style philanthropy that buys safety from pitchforks and a populist state. Moral fervour makes you look caring, so others want to work with you. These beliefs are cheap talk that signals club membership. Timur Kuran's preference falsification means people say what helps them get ahead. All of this needs intellectual soft-headedness: a broad doctor-engineer class with little social science or humanities, where few can call out the claims.
core_ideas.quote: To buy a Louis Vuitton is at least expensive. Here it's talk. Talk is free.

core_ideas.concept: We Signal Virtue to Ourselves, and Social Media Locks It In
core_ideas.explanation: Amit argues that most holders of luxury beliefs mean well. They lie to themselves as much as to others, and holding the right opinion stands in for doing good. Social media makes it worse. You join a tribe for belonging, accept its dogmas, attack outsiders, then attack insiders for impurity, which is why most cancellation comes from your own side. Once you have said something publicly, ego makes you double down. Amit read Marx and Engels at 17 and said silly things. With screenshots following him forever, he might never have grown out of them.
core_ideas.quote: Then I feel the incentive to double down on them for ego reasons, and then I become that person. I don't have that intellectual growth I might otherwise have.

core_ideas.explanation: Thomas Sowell's diagnosis, which Amit reads aloud. The prevailing vision offers believers a state of grace. Agreeing makes you morally superior, and disagreeing is treated as sin to be exposed, not error to be argued with. Amit's takeaway is that this is old and hardwired, not just a social media problem: we want to belong to a tribe and keep displaying our virtue.
core_ideas.quote: Those who accept this vision are deemed to be not merely factually correct, but morally on a higher plane. Put differently, those who disagree with the prevailing vision are seen as being not merely in error, but in sin.

core_ideas.concept: Be Firm on Values, Open on Facts
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's closing advice. Don't swallow any tribe's dogma from A to Z, and you don't need an opinion on everything after 30 seconds of thought. Hold your values firmly, but treat the facts of a complex world with humility and listen to people who disagree.
core_ideas.quote: When it comes to values, be firm on your values. When it comes to the facts of the world, the world is deeply complex. Be open, listen to people who disagree with you. That's the only way to grow.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay asks why they are colour-coordinated in shades of blue. Amit: 'Well, you know, maybe we both love the blues.'

Ajay turns Amit's Spotify discovery into a Bayes' theorem problem (working back from track to genre). Amit protests: 'Ajay, I'm talking about art, I'm talking about music, I'm talking about the soul.'
Ajay introduces the topic: 'there's an English word luxury like Louis Vuitton and Indian hotels, and there is a word like beliefs, which is like Bayes theorem and trigonometry.'
After Ajay picks 'Shallow' as his 2018 song, Amit: 'You and I should perform Shallow sometime. I'll do the high parts.'
Ajay says 32 years out is a practical horizon for their editor Nomsita. Amit: 'Thirty-two years later she'll be younger than you are now.'
Amit corrects himself from 'prostitutes' to 'sex workers', then takes it back: 'You and I are prostitutes, we're selling our services for money... I do a lot of things free even. So I'm even worse.'
In the price-control thought experiment, Amit tells viewers to pause the video and think, then freezes on camera: 'Have you paused? I just did statue...'
The running 'under my chair' gag: Amit keeps saying links are in the show notes 'under my chair', and finally wonders aloud what else is down there.
Amit, after a long tirade: 'Ajay, I have ranted and raved, which is my elite privilege. It is a luxury that I get to enjoy.'
Ajay begins his analysis: 'I'm a card-carrying economist, okay, and here is my card.'
Amit: 'Those who signal the most virtue possess the least. You know, and I have found this to be true especially of men, so watch out.'
The 'gentle reader' running joke. Amit mid-sentence: 'dear listener, dear reader. We are not listeners, we are readers.'
Amit on instant opinions: 'You've thought about that for thirty seconds. I have read about it for thirty years... and we are supposed to, on Twitter, be on equal ground.'

Shoegaze: the alt-rock genre named after guitarists who stood still on stage staring at their effects pedals. Amit found it via Galaxie 500, Dean Wareham's band before Luna, which he could never find in 90s India.
Gandhi's test, which both hosts take inspiration from: whenever you think of a policy, first ask what it does to the poor.

'Hamara socialism achha tha': Amit mimics older Seen and the Unseen guests nostalgic for the socialist era. One guest even lamented the Soviet Union's collapse, which Amit calls the best thing that happened to all of us.
Ajay's Communist Manifesto exercise: compare its closing program for action with modern India, which in many ways is the communist paradise Marx and Engels wanted.
Yes Minister: Amit invokes the line 'we must do something, this is something, let's do it' to describe intellectually lazy elite policymaking.
Raees: Amit's criticism of Shah Rukh Khan's 'terrible film', where the bootlegger treats the prohibition-seeking politician as an enemy. In real life, Amit says, the bootlegger funds him.
Hansie Cronje: Amit contrasts the match-fixing era with today, when cricketers earn so much that they have less incentive to wreck their careers.
Section 377: the law that effectively criminalised homosexuality, now struck down, which enabled the Matunga extortion racket.
Timur Kuran's preference falsification: Ajay cites it as one reason people profess beliefs that help them get ahead.
Amit's twist on 'the better angels of our nature': social media 'plays to the worst demons of our nature, as it were, instead of the better angels.'
